summary.text: A sample space is the set of all possible outcomes or results of an experiment or random trial.
A subset of the sample space is an event, and the outcomes must be mutually exclusive: if one occurs, no other one does.
It is one of three components of a probability model, alongside a set of possible events and a probability assigned to each event.

facts.label: Other names
facts.value: Sample description space, possibility space, outcome space

facts.label: Common labels
facts.value: S, Ω, or U for universal set

facts.label: Two dice
facts.value: 36 equally likely ordered pairs of outcomes

facts.label: Sum of five
facts.value: Four of the 36 pairs add to five

facts.label: Infinite example
facts.value: A light bulb's lifetime, with sample space from 0 to infinity

items.prompt: You flip a coin and only care whether it lands heads or tails. Should today's weather be part of your list of possible results?

options.label: Yes, because every detail of the trial is a result
Yes, because the weather could change the flip
No, because irrelevant information is removed
No, because weather cannot ever be recorded

items.explain: The sample space needs the right granularity for what the experimenter cares about, so irrelevant information such as the weather is left out.

items.prompt: You draw one card from a standard deck and want a sample space that describes each individual card. Which description works?

options.label: Just the ranks, from Ace through King
Just the four suits of the deck
Only whether the card is right-side up
Pairs combining a rank with a suit

items.explain: Ranks alone or suits alone are possible sample spaces, but describing each individual card takes both, giving fifty-two equally likely outcomes.

items.prompt: Two fair six-sided dice are rolled in a board game. What is the chance that the two numbers add up to five?

options.label: 1 in 11, since there are 11 possible sums
1 in 6, since each die has six faces
5 in 36, one for each unit of the sum
4 in 36, since four of the pairs work

items.explain: The 36 ordered pairs are equally likely, and four of them sum to five, so the probability is 4/36. The 11 possible sums are not equally likely, so counting sums alone misleads.

items.prompt: For one die roll, a student lists the possible results as 'the roll is even' and 'the roll is greater than 3'. What is wrong with this list?

options.label: Both can occur at once, so they are not mutually exclusive
There are too few results to make a proper list
The results are not equally likely to occur
Dice results cannot be written as words

items.explain: Outcomes must be mutually exclusive, but a roll of 4 makes both listed results occur at the same time.

items.prompt: A thumb tack is tossed many times and lands either point up or point down. Why is it a poor idea to just give each of the two results a chance of one half?

options.label: Because a tack can land in only one way
Nothing physical suggests the two results are equally likely
Because a tack has a different weight than a coin
Because two results must always be equally likely

items.explain: Equal likelihood suits cases like fair dice, but a thumb tack has no physical symmetry to suggest the two results are equally likely.

items.prompt: One die roll has six possible results. The group of results 'two, four, or six' is picked out. How does it relate to the full list of possible results?

options.label: It is a larger list that includes the full one
It is a single result of its own
It is a subset of the full list, called an event
It is a separate list with no shared results

items.explain: A subset of the sample space is an event, and the event occurs if the outcome of the experiment is included in it.
